column1: # Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam — Hadith 33: “The burden of proof is on the claimant”

column2: From Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both): The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “If people were given according to their claims, men would claim the wealth and the blood of others. But the burden of proof is on the claimant, and the oath is on the one who denies.”
A good (ḥasan) hadith, reported in this form by al-Bayhaqī and others; part of it is in the two Ṣaḥīḥs.
The core of this hadith was recorded by al-Bukhārī and Muslim in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from the hadith of Ibn Jurayj, from Ibn Abī Mulaykah, from Ibn ʿAbbās,
from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: “If people were given according to their claims, people would claim the blood and the wealth of men; but the oath is on the defendant.”
They also recorded it through the narration of Nāfiʿ ibn ʿUmar al-Jumaḥī, from Ibn Abī Mulaykah, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that the Prophet ﷺ decreed that the oath is on the defendant.
The wording in which the Shaykh gave it had been given before him by Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ in al-Aḥādīth al-Kulliyyah, who said: Al-Bayhaqī reported it with a good chain.
Al-Ismāʿīlī recorded it in his Ṣaḥīḥ through the narration of al-Walīd ibn Muslim: Ibn Jurayj told us, from Ibn Abī Mulaykah, from Ibn ʿAbbās,

that the Prophet ﷺ said: “If people were given according to their claims, men would claim the blood and the wealth of men; but the burden of proof is on the one who makes the demand, and the oath is on the one against whom it is made.”
Al-Shāfiʿī reported: Muslim ibn Khālid informed us, from Ibn Jurayj, from Ibn Abī Mulaykah, from Ibn ʿAbbās,
that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “The burden of proof is on the claimant.” Al-Shāfiʿī said: And I think — though I do not affirm it — that he said: “and the oath is on the defendant.”

Muḥammad ibn ʿUmar ibn Lubābah, the Andalusian jurist, reported from ʿUthmān ibn Ayyūb al-Andalusī — whom he described as a man of virtue — from Ghāzī ibn Qays, from Ibn Abī Mulaykah, from Ibn ʿAbbās, from the Prophet ﷺ, and he mentioned this hadith,

saying: “But the burden of proof is on whoever makes a claim, and the oath is on whoever denies.” Ghāzī ibn Qays al-Andalusī was a senior and righteous man who heard from Mālik, Ibn Jurayj and their generation. Ibn Jurayj has dropped out of this chain. And Allah knows best.

Imam Aḥmad and Abū ʿUbayd cited as evidence that the Prophet ﷺ said: “The burden of proof is on the claimant, and the oath is on the one who denies.” This shows that in their view the wording is authentic and may be used as proof. There are many hadiths with this meaning.
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from al-Ashʿath ibn Qays, who said: I had a dispute with a man over a well, and we took our dispute to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

“Your two witnesses, or his oath.” I said: Then he will swear and not care. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Whoever swears an oath by which he gains wealth, lying in it, will meet Allah while He is angry with him.”

Then Allah sent down confirmation of that, and he recited this verse: “Those who sell the covenant of Allah and their oaths for a small price…” [Āl ʿImrān 3:77]. In a narration of Muslim's, after his words, “Then he will swear,” he said: “You have nothing but that.”
Muslim also recorded something with its meaning from the hadith of Wāʾil ibn Ḥujr, from the Prophet ﷺ.
Al-Tirmidhī recorded, from the hadith of al-ʿArzamī, from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Prophet ﷺ

said in his sermon: “The burden of proof is on the claimant, and the oath is on the defendant.” He said: Its chain has been criticised, and al-ʿArzamī is considered weak in hadith because of his memory.
Al-Dāraquṭnī recorded it through the narration of Muslim ibn Khālid al-Zanjī — who has some weakness — from Ibn Jurayj, from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb,

from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: “The burden of proof is on the claimant, and the oath is on the one who denies, except in the qasāmah [the fifty oaths sworn over a slain man].”
The ḥuffāẓ reported it from Ibn Jurayj, from ʿAmr, in mursal form.
He also recorded it through the narration of Mujāhid, from Ibn ʿUmar, that the Prophet ﷺ said in his sermon on the day of the Conquest:
“The defendant has the better right to the oath, unless proof is established.” Al-Ṭabarānī recorded it too, in his version from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ, and its chain has been criticised.
Al-Dāraquṭnī recorded this meaning by several weak routes.

Ḥajjāj al-Ṣawwāf reported from Ḥumayd ibn Hilāl, from Zayd ibn Thābit, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ decreed: “Whenever a man makes a demand against another man, the one against whom it is made has the better right to the oath.”

Abū ʿUbayd and al-Bayhaqī recorded it, and its narrators are trustworthy, except that I do not think Ḥumayd ibn Hilāl met Zayd ibn Thābit. Al-Dāraquṭnī recorded it with the addition: “without witnesses.”
Al-Nasāʾī recorded, from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: Two disputants came to the Prophet ﷺ, and one of them claimed a right against the other. The Prophet ﷺ said to the claimant:
“Bring your proof.” He said: Messenger of Allah, I have no proof. So he said to the other: “Swear by Allah, besides whom there is no god, that he has nothing owed by you or held by you.”
It has been narrated that ʿUmar wrote to Abū Mūsā: The burden of proof is on the claimant, and the oath is on the one who denies.
Zayd ibn Thābit judged by this against ʿUmar in favour of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, and neither of them objected.
Qatādah said: The decisive judgement (faṣl al-khiṭāb) given to Dāwūd (peace be upon him) is that the burden of proof is on the claimant, and the oath is on the one who denies.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: The people of knowledge are agreed that the burden of proof is on the claimant and the oath is on the defendant. He said: The meaning of his words, “The burden of proof is on the claimant,” is that by it he becomes entitled to what he claimed,

since it is incumbent on him and he is held to it; and the meaning of his words, “The oath is on the defendant,” is that by it he is cleared, since it is incumbent on him and he is held to it in every case. End of quotation.
The jurists of our [Ḥanbalī] school and the Shāfiʿīs have differed over how to define the claimant and the defendant.
Some said: The claimant is the one of the two disputants who is left alone if he keeps silent, and the defendant is the one of them who is not left alone if he keeps silent.
Others said: The claimant is the one who asserts something hidden, contrary to the original state of things or to what is apparent, and the defendant is the reverse.

On this they built a question. If a disbelieving husband and wife become Muslim before consummation and then disagree, the husband saying, We became Muslim together, so our marriage stands, and the wife saying,

No, one of us became Muslim first, so the marriage is dissolved: if we say that the claimant is the one left alone when he keeps silent, the woman is the claimant, and the husband's word is accepted, because he is the defendant,

since he is not left alone if he keeps silent. But if we say that the claimant is the one who asserts something hidden, the claimant here is the husband, since becoming Muslim at the same moment is contrary to what is apparent; so the woman's word is accepted,
because the apparent is on her side.
As for a trustee who claims that the thing in his keeping was destroyed — such as a depositary who claims that the deposit was destroyed — some said that he is a claimant,
because the original state of things is contrary to what he claims; and he does not need proof only because the depositor entrusted him, and entrusting him entails accepting his word.

Others said: The claimant who needs proof is the one who claims in order to be given, by his claim, the wealth or the blood of others, as the hadith mentions; a trustee does not make a claim in order to be given anything. Others said: Rather, he is a defendant,
because if he keeps silent he is not left alone but must give an answer; and the depositor is the claimant,
because if he keeps silent he is left alone.
If the trustee claims to have returned the trust to the one who entrusted him with it,
most hold that his word is accepted in this too, as with a claim of destruction.
Al-Awzāʿī said: His word is not accepted, because he is a claimant.

Mālik, and Aḥmad in one reported position, said: If his receipt of the trust is established by proof, his word that he returned it is not accepted without proof. Some of the scholars of our school explained this on the grounds that calling witnesses to the handing over of rights established by proof is obligatory,
so that failing to do so is negligence, which makes him liable. A group of them likewise said of handing over an orphan's property to him: the guardian must have proof,
because Allah the Exalted commanded that witnesses be called to it, so it is obligatory.
The jurists have differed on this subject in two views.
One is that the burden of proof is always on the claimant

and the oath always on the defendant. This is the view of Abū Ḥanīfah, and a group of jurists and hadith scholars, such as al-Bukhārī, agreed with him. They applied it consistently to every claim, even to the qasāmah, saying that none but the defendant swears. They held that judgement is not to be given on one witness and an oath,
because the oath is never on the claimant; and they held that the oath is not to be turned back on the claimant,
because it lies only on the side of the one who denies, the defendant.

On the question of the qasāmah they cited what Saʿīd ibn ʿUbayd reported: Bushayr ibn Yasār al-Anṣārī told us, from Sahl ibn Abī Ḥathmah, that he told him that a party of their people set out for Khaybar and split up there, and they found one of them slain. He mentioned the hadith, which includes:

The Prophet ﷺ said: “Bring me proof against whoever killed him.” They said: We have no proof. He said: “Then they will swear.” They said: We will not accept the oaths of the Jews. The Prophet ﷺ was loath to let his blood go unrequited, so he paid his blood money with a hundred of the camels of zakāh. Al-Bukhārī recorded it,

and Muslim recorded it in abridged form without giving it in full. But this narration conflicts with the narration of Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd al-Anṣārī, from Bushayr ibn Yasār, from Sahl ibn Abī Ḥathmah, who told the story of the slain man and said in it:
They told the Messenger of Allah ﷺ of the killing of ʿAbdullāh ibn Sahl, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

“Let fifty of you swear against a man of them, and he will be handed over to you by his rope.” This is the well-known, established narration, recorded in full and in its own wording in the two Ṣaḥīḥs.

The imams among the ḥuffāẓ have stated that the narration of Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd is more authentic than that of Saʿīd ibn ʿUbayd al-Ṭāʾī, for he is greater, more learned and of better memory; he is one of the people of Madīnah, and knows their hadith better than the Kūfans do.

Imam Aḥmad mentioned how Saʿīd ibn ʿUbayd differed from Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd in this hadith, and waved his hand dismissively, saying: That is nothing; he narrated it in line with what the Kūfans say. And he said: I follow the hadith of the Madinans, Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd.
Al-Nasāʾī said: We know of no one who corroborated Saʿīd ibn ʿUbayd in his narration from Bushayr ibn Yasār. Muslim said in his book al-Tamyīz: Saʿīd ibn ʿUbayd did not preserve it accurately,
because in all the reports the Prophet ﷺ asks them for a qasāmah of fifty oaths,
and in none of their reports does the Prophet ﷺ ask them for proof. Saʿīd left out the qasāmah, and the reports' agreement against him decides that he erred; and Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd contradicted him.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said of the narration of Saʿīd ibn ʿUbayd: This is the narration of the people of Iraq from Bushayr ibn Yasār. The narration of the people of Madīnah from him is more firmly established; they knew him more closely, and their transmission is more authentic in the view of the people of knowledge.
I say: Saʿīd ibn ʿUbayd abridged the story of the qasāmah, which is preserved in the hadith. Al-Nasāʾī recorded, from the hadith of ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father,
from his grandfather, that the Prophet ﷺ asked the next of kin of the slain man for two witnesses against whoever had killed him. He said: And where am I to find two witnesses?
He said: “Then swear fifty oaths of qasāmah.” He said: How can I swear to what I do not know? He said:

“Then have fifty of them swear oaths of qasāmah.” This hadith reconciles the two narrations of Saʿīd ibn ʿUbayd and Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd: each of them left out part of the story. Saʿīd left out the claimants' qasāmah, and Yaḥyā left out the request for proof before the qasāmah was asked for. And Allah knows best.
As for the question of one witness with an oath, those who reject judging by one witness and an oath cited the hadith, “Your two witnesses, or his oath,” and his words ﷺ, “You have nothing but that.”

Al-Qāḍī Ismāʿīl the Mālikī criticised this wording, saying: Manṣūr alone narrated it from Abū Wāʾil, and all the other narrators contradicted him, saying that he asked him: “Do you have proof or not?”
And proof is not confined to two witnesses
but covers everything that makes the truth clear.

Someone else said: By “your two witnesses” he may have meant any two kinds of evidence that testify for the claimant to the soundness of his claim and by which the truth becomes clear. That includes the testimony of two men, the testimony of a man with two women, and the testimony of one witness with an oath. Allah, Glorified is He, has made the claimant's oaths take the place of witnesses in liʿān, the mutual cursing of spouses.

His words at the end of the hadith, “You have nothing but that,” were not meant as a general negation but as a specific one, negating what the claimant wanted: that his word be accepted without proof.
So he denied him that and refused it to him. Likewise his words in the other hadith, “but the oath is on the defendant,” mean only the oath unaccompanied by testimony,
as the beginning of the hadith shows, namely his words: “If people were given according to their claims, men would claim the blood and the wealth of men.” This shows that his words,

“The oath is on the defendant,” refer only to the oath that ends the dispute when there is no proof. The oath that establishes a right alongside testimony is another kind, and it is established by another sunnah.

As for turning the oath back on the claimant, the well-known position of Aḥmad agrees with Abū Ḥanīfah's: it is not turned back. Aḥmad cited the hadith, “The oath is on the defendant.” In the narration of Abū Ṭālib from him, he said: It is not far-fetched that he should be told:

Swear and be entitled. A group of the later scholars of our school chose this, and it is the view of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and Abū ʿUbayd. It is narrated from a group of the Companions, and there is a hadith on it as marfūʿ (attributed to the Prophet ﷺ) which al-Dāraquṭnī recorded, though its chain is open to question.
Abū ʿUbayd said: This is not removing the oath from its proper place, for removing it would mean not giving judgement by the oath against the defendant at all.

But when it is adjudged against him and he is content with the oath of the other party, he has passed judgement on himself; for had he wished, he would have sworn, been cleared, and had the claim against him dismissed.

The second view on the question is that the side of the stronger of the two disputants is preferred, and the oath is placed on his side. This is the position of Mālik, and al-Qāḍī Abū Yaʿlā likewise stated in his Khilāf that it is the position of Aḥmad. On this basis the questions mentioned above — judging by the qasāmah and by one witness with an oath — are accounted for:

when the claimant's side in the qasāmah is strengthened by lawth (circumstantial evidence against the accused), the oath is placed on his side and judgement is given for him by it; and likewise when the claimant produces one witness, his side is strengthened, so he swears along with the witness and judgement is given for him.
These scholars have two ways of answering the hadith, “The burden of proof is on the claimant.” One is that these cases are excepted from its general sense by evidence.
The second is that his words, “The burden of proof is on the claimant,” are not general,

because what is meant is the familiar sort of claimant, one who has no argument but his claim, as in his words: “If people were given according to their claims, men would claim the blood and the wealth of others.” A claimant who has some argument strengthening his claim is not included in this hadith.

A third way is that proof is anything that makes clear the soundness of the claimant's claim and testifies to his truthfulness; so lawth with the qasāmah is proof, and one witness with an oath is proof.
A fourth way, which some have taken, is to challenge the authenticity of this wording, I mean his words,
“The burden of proof is on the claimant,” and to say that what is established is only his words, “The oath is on the defendant.”

His words, “If people were given according to their claims, people would claim the blood and the wealth of others,” show that one who claims blood or wealth must have proof pointing to what he claims. Included in the general sense of this is that if someone claims that a man killed the person he inherits from,

and he has nothing but the slain man's words at his death, “So-and-so wounded me,” that is not sufficient, and by itself it does not count as lawth. This is the view of the majority, contrary to the Mālikīs, who counted it as lawth with which the next of kin swear the qasāmah and become entitled to the blood.

Also included in its general sense is a man who accuses his wife of adultery and performs liʿān against her: her blood does not become lawful merely through the liʿān. This is the view of most, contrary to al-Shāfiʿī, and al-Jūzajānī chose his view because of the apparent sense of His words, Mighty and Majestic is He:

“And it will avert the punishment from her if she testifies four times by Allah…” [al-Nūr 24:8]. Some of the former group understood the punishment as imprisonment, saying: If she does not perform liʿān, she is imprisoned until she confesses or performs it. But this is open to question.
If a woman claims that a man forced her into fornication, the majority hold that nothing is established against him by her claim.
Ashhab, of the Mālikīs, said: She is owed the dower on her oath; another of them said: She is owed the dower without an oath. All this applies when she is a woman of standing

and makes the claim against a suspect of whom such a claim is plausible. If the man accused of it is one of the righteous, there are two reported positions of Mālik on whether she receives the prescribed punishment for slander.

Shurayḥ and Iyās ibn Muʿāwiyah used to judge disputed property merely by circumstantial signs pointing to the truthfulness of one of the two disputants. Shurayḥ judged the case of a cat's kitten claimed by two women,
each saying: It is my cat's kitten. Shurayḥ said: Put it with this one. If she settles, lets her milk flow and stretches out, it is hers; but if she runs off, hisses and bristles, it is not hers.
Ibn Qutaybah said:
By isbaṭarrat he means that she stretched out to suckle it, and izbaʾarrat means that she bristled and fluffed up her fur.
Abū Bakr al-Shāmī, of the Shāfiʿīs, used to judge in a similar way, and Ibn ʿAqīl, of our school, preferred his view.

It is narrated from al-Shāfiʿī and Aḥmad that they approved of the word of trackers (qāfah) in cases of stolen property and acted on it. Ibn Manṣūr transmitted from Aḥmad: If the owner of the crops says,
Your sheep spoiled my crops at night, the tracks are examined; if there are no tracks of his sheep in the crops, the owner of the crops must bring proof.
Isḥāq ibn Rāhawayh said as Aḥmad said,
because he is a claimant. This shows that they both agreed that seeing the sheep's tracks is enough, and that proof is required only when there are no tracks.
His words, “and the oath is on the defendant,” show that anyone against whom a claim is made and who denies it must take the oath. This is the view of most jurists.

Mālik said: The oath is binding on the one who denies only if there has been some kind of dealing between the two disputants, for fear that foolish people would humiliate men of rank by demanding their oaths.

In his view, if someone claims that a man seized his property or stole from him, and the defendant is not suspected of such things, the defendant is not made to swear. This is also related from al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad

and Ḥumayd ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, and some related it from the Seven Jurists of Madīnah. If he is a man of virtue, one to whom no such thing would be imputed, the claimant is to be disciplined, in Mālik's view. From his words,
“The oath is on the defendant,” it is inferred that the claimant owes no oath, only proof. This is the view of most.
It is narrated from ʿAlī that he made the claimant swear, along with his proof, that his witnesses had testified truly. Shurayḥ also did this,
as did ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUtbah, Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn Abī Laylā, Sawwār al-ʿAnbarī, ʿUbaydullāh ibn al-Ḥasan and Muḥammad ibn ʿAbdullāh al-Anṣārī; it is also narrated from al-Nakhaʿī.
Isḥāq said: If the judge has doubts, it becomes obligatory.
Muhannā asked Imam Aḥmad about this question, and Aḥmad said: ʿAlī did it. He said to him: Is this right?
He said: ʿAlī did it. Al-Qāḍī [Abū Yaʿlā] therefore recorded this as a reported position of Aḥmad, but he restricted it to a claim against someone absent or against a child. That is not correct,

because ʿAlī made the claimant swear along with his proof against someone who was present with him. These scholars say: This oath is to strengthen the claim when it has been weakened by doubts about the witnesses, like the oath with a single witness.

Some early scholars also used to make the witnesses swear when they had doubts about them, among them Sawwār al-ʿAnbarī, judge of al-Baṣrah. Al-Qāḍī Abū Yaʿlā, of our school, allowed this to the official who hears complaints of injustice (wālī al-maẓālim), though not to judges.
Ibn ʿAbbās said of a woman who testifies about breastfeeding: She is made to swear. Imam Aḥmad adopted this.

The Qurʾān indicates that witnesses are to be made to swear when there is doubt about their testimony, in the case of a bequest made on a journey, in His words, Exalted is He: “O you who believe, the testimony between you, when death approaches one of you at the time of making a bequest, [shall be that of] two just men from among you, or two others from outside you…” up to His words:

“…and let them both swear by Allah, if you are in doubt: ‘We will not sell it for any price, even if he be a relative, nor will we conceal the testimony of Allah’” [al-Māʾidah 5:106]. In the view of most of the Salaf, acting on this verse has not been abrogated. Abū Mūsā acted on it,

as did Ibn Masʿūd, and ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbās gave fatwas by it. It is the position of Shurayḥ, al-Nakhaʿī, Ibn Abī Laylā, Sufyān, al-Awzāʿī, Aḥmad, Abū ʿUbayd and others. They said: The testimony of disbelievers is accepted concerning the bequests of Muslims made on a journey, and the two of them are made to swear along with their testimony.
Is their oath part of completing the testimony, so that judgement is not given on their testimony without an oath, or is it a precaution taken when there is doubt?
Either is possible. The scholars of our school made it a condition, and that is the apparent sense of what is narrated from Abū Mūsā and others.

A group of the Salaf held that the oath with a single witness is a precaution: if the judge sees fit to be satisfied with the single witness, because his probity is evident and his truthfulness plain, he accepts his testimony without the claimant's oath.

His words, “But if it is discovered that the two were guilty of sin, then let two others stand in their place, from those who have a claim against them, the two nearest of kin, and let them swear by Allah: ‘Our testimony is truer than their testimony’” [al-Māʾidah 5:107], show that if a flaw appears in the testimony of the disbelievers,
the heirs of the deceased swear to their treachery and lying, and become entitled to what they swore to. This is the view of Mujāhid and others among the Salaf.

The reasoning is that the oath lies on the side of the stronger of the two disputants. Here the heirs' claim has been strengthened by the disbelieving witnesses' lie coming to light, so the oath is turned back on the claimants:

they swear along with the lawth and become entitled to what they claimed, just as the next of kin swear in the qasāmah along with lawth and thereby become entitled to the blood money — and to the blood as well, in the view of Mālik, Aḥmad and others.

Ibn Masʿūd judged the case of a Muslim man whom death overtook. He appointed two Muslim men who were with him as executors, handed over to them the property he had with him, and called disbelievers to witness his will. Then the two executors arrived and handed part of the property over to the heirs,

concealing part of it. Then the disbelievers arrived and testified against them about the property they had concealed. So he summoned the two Muslim executors and made them swear that no more had been handed to them than they had handed over. Then he summoned the disbelievers, who testified and swore to their testimony.

Then he ordered the heirs of the deceased to swear that what the Jews and Christians had testified to was true. They swore, and he gave judgement against the two executors for what the heirs had sworn to. This was during the caliphate of ʿUthmān, and Ibn Masʿūd interpreted the verse in this way.

It is as though he set the executors' oath against that of the disbelieving witnesses so that the two cancelled each other out. The heirs were left with the disbelievers' testimony, so they swore along with it and became entitled, because their side had been tipped in their favour by the disbelievers' testimony. So he placed the oath with the stronger of the two disputants and gave judgement by it.

The jurists differed over whether an oath may be required in all the rights of human beings, as al-Shāfiʿī holds and as in one reported position of Aḥmad; or only in matters where judgement is given on refusal to swear, as in another reported position of Aḥmad;
or only in what may validly be given up freely, as is the well-known position of Aḥmad;
or only in every claim that does not need two witnesses, as is related from Mālik.

As for the rights of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, some scholars said that no oath may be required in them in any case. This is the view of the scholars of our school and others; Aḥmad stated it explicitly concerning zakāh, and Ṭāwūs held it,

as did al-Thawrī, al-Ḥasan ibn Ṣāliḥ and others. Abū Ḥanīfah, Mālik, al-Layth and al-Shāfiʿī said: If he is suspected, he is made to swear. The same is related from al-Shāfiʿī concerning someone who marries a woman unlawful for him

and then claims ignorance: he is made to swear to his claim. Isḥāq likewise said of a divorce pronounced while drunk: he swears that he was not in his right mind; and of a divorce pronounced in forgetfulness: he swears that he forgot.
Al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad and Sālim ibn ʿAbdullāh likewise said of a man who says to his wife, You are divorced, that he swears he did not mean a triple divorce by it, and she is returned to him.
Al-Ṭabarānī recorded, through the narration of Abū Hārūn al-ʿAbdī, from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, who said: Some Bedouins used to bring meat, and we had some misgivings about it.
We mentioned this to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he said: “Make them swear their most solemn oaths that they slaughtered it, then mention the name of Allah and eat.” Abū Hārūn is very weak.
As for someone entrusted with the rights of human beings, in cases where his word is accepted, does he owe an oath or not?
Scholars have three views on this. The first is that he owes no oath,
because the owner declared him truthful by entrusting him, and no oath is required where he has been believed; also by analogy with the judge. This is the view of al-Ḥārith al-ʿUklī.

The second is that he owes the oath, because he is one who denies and so falls under the general sense of his words, “and the oath is on the one who denies.” This is the view of Shurayḥ, Abū Ḥanīfah, al-Shāfiʿī, Mālik in one reported position, and most of the scholars of our school.
The third is that he owes no oath unless he is suspected. This is Aḥmad's explicit position, and the view of Mālik in one reported position, because he was entrusted, as mentioned above.
But when some sign appears that is at odds with a state of trust, the very meaning of trust has been undermined.

His words, “The burden of proof is on the claimant, and the oath is on the one who denies,” refer only to the case where someone claims against a man something which that man claims for himself, denying that it belongs to the one claiming it against him. That is why he said at the start of the hadith: “If people were given according to their claims, men would claim the blood and the wealth of others.”

Where, however, someone claims something with no one claiming it for himself and denying the claim, that is easier than the first case. The claimant here must still have proof, but less is accepted as proof here than in a claim against someone who claims the thing for himself and denies it.
Several questions bear this out.
One is lost property: if someone comes and describes it, it is handed over to him without proof, by agreement. Some, however, say that it may be handed over if his truthfulness seems most likely,
but that this is not obligatory, as al-Shāfiʿī and Abū Ḥanīfah hold; and some say that it must be handed over once a matching description is given, as Mālik and Aḥmad hold.

Another is spoils of war: if someone comes claiming that something among them was his and that the disbelievers had seized it, and he produces something that shows it is his, that is sufficient. Aḥmad was asked about this and was told: Does he need proof besides that?
He said: There must be some evidence showing that it is his; and if that is known, the commander hands it over to him.

Al-Khallāl reported, with his chain of narration, from al-Rukayn ibn al-Rabīʿ, from his father, who said: A horse of my brother's strayed at ʿAyn al-Tamr, and he saw it among Saʿd's tethered horses. He said: That is my horse. Saʿd said: Do you have proof?

He said: No, but I will call it and it will whinny. He called it and it whinnied, so he gave it to him. This may be because it had gone over to the enemy and the Muslims then captured it; or it may be that he knew it was a stray and it had been put among the stray animals, so that it is like lost property.
Another is property seized by force, when the injustice of the governors is known and the owner asks for it to be returned from the treasury. Abū al-Zinād said:

ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz used to return wrongfully taken property to its owners without conclusive proof. He was satisfied with little: if he recognised how a man had been wronged, he gave it back to him without requiring him to establish proof,
because he knew how the governors before him had oppressed the people. He exhausted the treasury of Iraq in returning wrongfully taken property, until money had to be carried there from al-Shām.

The scholars of our school have stated that, for property seized and found with highway robbers and thieves, a description from the one who claims it is sufficient, as with lost property. Al-Qāḍī mentioned this in his Khilāf, saying that it is the apparent sense of Aḥmad's words.
